newsitem.title: CHINA: China lambasts international human rights groups.
newsitem.headline: China lambasts international human rights groups.

text.p: China on Thursday condemned international watchdog groups for spreading baseless rumours on its human rights record and hailing common criminals as democracy fighters.
"Some so-called human rights groups abroad do not understand the real situation in China but frequently spread baseless rumours," Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Cui Tiankai told a news briefing.

"They frequently treat some criminal elements as democracy fighters and use these problems as a pretext to infringe on the independence of China's judiciary and interfere in China's internal affairs," Cui said.

"This is very wrong," he said when asked to comment on a threat by the wife of jailed dissident Liu Nianchun to stage demonstrations and a sit-down protest if her ailing husband were not allowed to seek medical treatment.

Liu's wife, Chu Hailan, wrote to the head of parliament and Beijing's mayor on March 8, demanding that Chinese authorities allow her husband to see a doctor before the end of the month, the New York-based group Human Rights in China said.
"I do not wish to see the illness of my husband worsen because of delays in medical treatment," Chu said in her letter, a copy of which was made available to Reuters by the group.
"If this happens, I will take all legitimate means, including litigation, demonstration, sit-down protest...to protect the rights of my husband," she said.
Chu said her husband, imprisoned in the Shuanghe labour camp in northeast China, suffered from intestinal problems, an enlarged lymph node and ulcers in his mouth.

In July, authorities ordered Liu to serve three years of re-education through labour for drafting a petition that urged the government to reassess its 1989 crackdown on student demonstrators in Beijing's Tiananmen Square.
Re-education through labour is a form of administrative punishment that can be imposed by authorities without a trial.
The 48-year-old dissident appealed the labour camp term, but a Beijing court rejected the motion last December.
Liu, who was active in the Democracy Wall movement in the early 1980s, was jailed for three years in 1981 for incitement and spreading counter-revolutionary propaganda, or subversion.
Western human rights activists say re-education through labour is used by authorities to remove dissidents from circulation without the publicity of a trial.
China, the world's most populous nation, argues it must give priority to protecting the rights of 1.2 billion people by providing them with food and shelter.

The wide gap in views on human rights has led to considerable tension between China and Western countries, particularly in the years since China called in the army to crush the 1989 democracy demonstrations.
In its annual report on human rights, the U.S. State Department accused Beijing of effectively silencing public dissent in 1996 through jailings, intimidation or exile.
The Hong Kong-based Information Centre of Human Rights and Democratic Movement in China said 42 pro-democracy activists were jailed in 1996.
